hints: Look closely at the solid curve with no inhibitor. At 1 the line is still rising steeply, but at 2 it has flattened into a plateau. What is in short supply in each part?

Compare the two inhibitor curves to the top curve. One curve eventually catches up to the same maximum rate at high substrate, the other stays low forever. Which inhibitor type can be outcompeted by adding more substrate?
walkthrough:
**Read points 1 and 2 on the normal curve**

At 1, adding more substrate makes the rate go up in a straight line. That tells you substrate is limiting, because there are still free active sites waiting for it.

At 2, adding more substrate makes no difference, the curve plateaus. That tells you all active sites are now saturated, so enzyme concentration is limiting.

**Read point 3 on the competitive inhibitor curve**

Point 3 is lower than the normal curve at the same substrate concentration, but with very high substrate it eventually reaches the same maximum rate.

This is classic competitive inhibition. The inhibitor blocks the active site, but extra substrate can outcompete it, so the inhibitor is what is slowing the rate at 3.

**Read point 4 on the non-competitive inhibitor curve**

Point 4 plateaus at a much lower maximum rate that never catches up, no matter how much substrate you add.

This is classic non-competitive inhibition. The inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes enzyme shape, effectively removing enzyme, so the inhibitor is limiting at 4.

options.A: Swaps 1 and 2. At 1 the rate rises with substrate, so substrate is limiting, not enzyme.
options.B: Swaps 1 and 2 and also swaps 3 and 4. Competitive inhibition can be overcome to reach normal Vmax, which is curve 3, not curve 4.
options.C: Correct. 1 is substrate limited, 2 is enzyme limited, 3 is limited by competitive inhibitor, 4 is limited by non-competitive inhibitor.
options.D: Gets 1 and 2 right but swaps 3 and 4. Curve 4 never reaches normal Vmax, so it must be non-competitive, not competitive.
